name: Introduce the formal notation used for MLP training (sets of neurons, potentials, outputs, weights, j<sub>←</sub> and j<sub>→</sub>) and define the activity of an MLP in this notation.
answer:
Architecture (recap): neurons are partitioned into layers numbered from 0 (input layer), neurons of the i-th layer are connected with all neurons of the (i+1)-st layer.

Notation:
• X – the set of input neurons, Y – the set of output neurons, Z – the set of all neurons (X, Y ⊆ Z);
• individual neurons are denoted by indices i, j, etc.;
• ξj – the inner potential of neuron j after the computation stops;
• yj – the output of neuron j after the computation stops (define y0 = 1 as the value of the formal unit input);
• wji – the weight of the connection from i to j (in particular wj0 is the weight of the connection from the formal unit input; the slide writes wj0 = −bj, where bj is the bias of neuron j);
• j← – the set of all i such that j is adjacent from i (there is an arc to j from i);
• j→ – the set of all i such that j is adjacent to i (there is an arc from j to i).

Activity:
• inner potential of neuron j: ξj = Σi∈j← wjiyi;
• each neuron j has an activation function σj (arbitrary differentiable);
• the state of a non-input neuron j ∈ Z ∖ X after the computation stops: yj = σj(ξj). Since yj depends on the configuration w and the input x, we sometimes write yj(w, x);
• the network computes a function from ℝ|X| to ℝ|Y|. Layer-wise computation: first, all input neurons are assigned the values of the input; in the ℓ-th step, all neurons of the ℓ-th layer are evaluated.
keyPoints: X input, Y output, Z all neurons
w_ji = weight of the connection from i to j; w_j0 = weight of the formal unit input y_0 = 1
j← = predecessors of j, j→ = successors of j
ξ_j = Σ_{i∈j←} w_ji y_i, y_j = σ_j(ξ_j) with differentiable σ_j
Network computes ℝ^|X| → ℝ^|Y| layer by layer

name: Define the training dataset and the (squared) error function of an MLP, and describe the batch gradient descent algorithm.
answer:
Training dataset: T = { (xk, dk) | k = 1, …, p }, where every xk ∈ ℝ|X| is an input vector and every dk ∈ ℝ|Y| is the desired network output. For every j ∈ Y, dkj denotes the desired output of neuron j for the network input xk, so dk = (dkj)j∈Y.

Error function:
E(w) = Σk=1..p Ek(w), where Ek(w) = ½ Σj∈Y (yj(w, xk) − dkj)2.
(This is just an example of an error function; other error functions come later.)

Batch algorithm (gradient descent): the algorithm computes a sequence of weight vectors w(0), w(1), w(2), …
• the weights in w(0) are randomly initialized to values close to 0;
• in step t + 1 (t = 0, 1, 2, …) the weights are computed as
wji(t+1) = wji(t) + Δwji(t), where Δwji(t) = −ε(t) · ∂E/∂wji(w(t))
is the weight update of wji in step t + 1 and 0 < ε(t) ≤ 1 is the learning rate in step t + 1.

Since ∂E/∂wji(w(t)) is a component of the gradient ∇E, the update can be written in vector form: w(t+1) = w(t) − ε(t) · ∇E(w(t)). The gradient points in the direction of the steepest increase of E, so the algorithm moves the weights against it. It is called batch because every step uses the error over the whole training set.
keyPoints: E(w) = Σ_k E_k(w), E_k(w) = ½ Σ_{j∈Y} (y_j(w, x_k) − d_kj)²
w^(0) random, close to 0
Δw_ji^(t) = −ε(t) · ∂E/∂w_ji (w^(t)), 0 < ε(t) ≤ 1 is the learning rate
Vector form: w^(t+1) = w^(t) − ε(t) ∇E(w^(t))

name: State the formulas for the gradient of the MLP error function (∂E/∂w<sub>ji</sub>, ∂E<sub>k</sub>/∂w<sub>ji</sub> and ∂E<sub>k</sub>/∂y<sub>j</sub> for output and hidden neurons) and derive the formula for ∂E<sub>k</sub>/∂w<sub>ji</sub> using the chain rule.
answer:
Formulas. For every weight wji:
∂E/∂wji = Σk=1..p ∂Ek/∂wji,
where for every k = 1, …, p
∂Ek/∂wji = ∂Ek/∂yj · σ′j(ξj) · yi,
and for every j ∈ Z ∖ X:
• ∂Ek/∂yj = yj − dkj for j ∈ Y (output neurons),
• ∂Ek/∂yj = Σr∈j→ ∂Ek/∂yr · σ′r(ξr) · wrj for j ∈ Z ∖ (Y ∪ X) (hidden neurons).
(Here all yj are in fact yj(w, xk).)

Derivation of ∂Ek/∂wji. The first equality holds because E = Σk Ek and differentiation is linear. Fix k and a weight wji. The weight wji influences Ek only through the potential ξj and thus through the output yj of neuron j. By the chain rule:
∂Ek/∂wji = ∂Ek/∂yj · ∂yj/∂wji = ∂Ek/∂yj · ∂yj/∂ξj · ∂ξj/∂wji = ∂Ek/∂yj · σ′j(ξj) · yi,
since
• ∂yj/∂ξj = ∂(σj(ξj))/∂ξj = σ′j(ξj),
• ∂ξj/∂wji = ∂(Σr∈j← wjryr)/∂wji = yi (only the term with r = i depends on wji).
keyPoints: ∂E/∂w_ji = Σ_k ∂E_k/∂w_ji
∂E_k/∂w_ji = ∂E_k/∂y_j · σ′_j(ξ_j) · y_i
Output neuron: ∂E_k/∂y_j = y_j − d_kj
Hidden neuron: ∂E_k/∂y_j = Σ_{r∈j→} ∂E_k/∂y_r · σ′_r(ξ_r) · w_rj
Chain rule through y_j and ξ_j: ∂y_j/∂ξ_j = σ′_j(ξ_j), ∂ξ_j/∂w_ji = y_i

name: Derive the backpropagation formulas for ∂E<sub>k</sub>/∂y<sub>j</sub>: first for an output neuron j ∈ Y (squared error), then for a hidden neuron. What do the formulas become when all activations are logistic sigmoids?
answer:
Output neuron j ∈ Y. With Ek = ½ Σr∈Y (yr − dkr)2:
∂Ek/∂yj = ∂(½ Σr∈Y (yr − dkr)2)/∂yj = yj − dkj
(only the term r = j depends on yj; the ½ cancels the 2).

Hidden neuron j ∉ Y. The output yj influences Ek only through the neurons r ∈ j→ to which j sends its output. By another application of the chain rule:
∂Ek/∂yj = Σr∈j→ ∂Ek/∂yr · ∂yr/∂yj = Σr∈j→ ∂Ek/∂yr · ∂yr/∂ξr · ∂ξr/∂yj = Σr∈j→ ∂Ek/∂yr · σ′r(ξr) · wrj,
since
• ∂yr/∂ξr = ∂(σr(ξr))/∂ξr = σ′r(ξr),
• ∂ξr/∂yj = ∂(Σs∈r← wrsys)/∂yj = wrj. □

The derivative for a hidden neuron is thus expressed through the derivatives of the neurons in the layer above – the error is propagated backwards.

Logistic sigmoid (historical special case). If yj = σj(ξj) = 1/(1 + e−ξj) for all j ∈ Z, then σ′j(ξj) = yj(1 − yj), and thus for all j ∈ Z ∖ X:
• ∂Ek/∂yj = yj − dkj for j ∈ Y,
• ∂Ek/∂yj = Σr∈j→ ∂Ek/∂yr · yr(1 − yr) · wrj for j ∈ Z ∖ (Y ∪ X).
The derivative of the activation is then obtained directly from the neuron's output computed in the forward pass.
keyPoints: Output: differentiate ½ Σ (y_r − d_kr)² w.r.t. y_j → y_j − d_kj
Hidden: chain rule over all successors r ∈ j→
∂y_r/∂ξ_r = σ′_r(ξ_r) and ∂ξ_r/∂y_j = w_rj
Result: ∂E_k/∂y_j = Σ_{r∈j→} ∂E_k/∂y_r · σ′_r(ξ_r) · w_rj
Logistic sigmoid: σ′_j(ξ_j) = y_j(1 − y_j)

name: Describe the complete algorithm that computes the gradient ∂E/∂w<sub>ji</sub> of an MLP (forward pass, backward pass, accumulation), including the order in which backpropagation evaluates neurons and why this order works.
answer:
Goal: compute ∂E/∂wji = Σk=1..p ∂Ek/∂wji for all weights.

Algorithm:
Initialize Eji := 0 for all weights (by the end of the computation Eji = ∂E/∂wji).
For every k = 1, …, p do:
1. forward pass: compute yj = yj(w, xk) for all j ∈ Z;
2. backward pass: compute ∂Ek/∂yj for all j ∈ Z using backpropagation (below);
3. compute ∂Ek/∂wji for all wji using ∂Ek/∂wji := ∂Ek/∂yj · σ′j(ξj) · yi;
4. Eji := Eji + ∂Ek/∂wji.
The resulting Eji equals ∂E/∂wji.

Backpropagation – compute ∂Ek/∂yj for all j ∈ Z as follows:
• if j ∈ Y, then ∂Ek/∂yj = yj − dkj;
• if j ∈ Z ∖ (Y ∪ X), then, assuming that j is in the ℓ-th layer and that ∂Ek/∂yr has already been computed for all neurons in the (ℓ+1)-st layer, compute
∂Ek/∂yj = Σr∈j→ ∂Ek/∂yr · σ′r(ξr) · wrj.

Why the order works: all neurons r ∈ j→ belong to the (ℓ+1)-st layer, so proceeding from the output layer downwards, layer by layer, every value needed on the right-hand side is already available. The forward pass must come first because the backward pass uses the values yj and ξj (for σ′r(ξr)) computed in it.
keyPoints: Initialize accumulators E_ji := 0; loop over all training examples k
Forward pass: compute all y_j for input x_k
Backward pass: ∂E_k/∂y_j from the output layer down
∂E_k/∂w_ji := ∂E_k/∂y_j · σ′_j(ξ_j) · y_i, then E_ji += ∂E_k/∂w_ji
Works because all r ∈ j→ lie in the next layer, already processed

name: What is the time complexity of one gradient computation in the batch algorithm? Give the proof sketch. What can be said about the speed of convergence, and what does the XOR illustration of gradient descent show?
answer:
Claim. The computation of ∂E/∂wji(w(t−1)) stops in time linear in the size of the network times the size of the training set (assuming unit cost of operations, including the computation of σ′r(ξr) for a given ξr).

Proof sketch. The algorithm does the following p times:
1. forward pass, i.e. computes yj(w, xk);
2. backpropagation, i.e. computes ∂Ek/∂yj;
3. computes ∂Ek/∂wji and adds it to Eji (a constant-time operation per weight in the unit cost framework).
Steps 1–3 take linear time w.r.t. the number of network weights: in the forward pass every weight is used once (in the sum ξj = Σ wjiyi), in the backward pass every weight wrj appears once in the sums over r ∈ j→, and step 3 does constant work per weight. Repeating this for p examples gives time linear in (number of weights) × p.

Convergence. This bounds only the cost of one gradient computation (one step). The speed of convergence of the gradient descent – how many steps are needed – cannot be estimated.

XOR illustration (figure). A small network is trained on XOR by gradient descent. The inputs are not linearly separable in the input representation, but the figure tracks how the hidden representation (y1, y2) of the four training points moves during training (after 15, 30, 45, 60 epochs) until the two classes end up on different sides of a line – the final decision boundary of the output neuron. Gradient descent thus gradually learns hidden features that make the problem linearly separable.
keyPoints: Time linear in (size of the network) × (size of the training set)
Unit cost of operations, including σ′
Per example: forward pass, backpropagation, per-weight update of E_ji – each linear in the number of weights
The number of gradient-descent steps (speed of convergence) cannot be estimated
XOR figure: hidden representation moves until the classes are linearly separable
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 94–95 (slide 95 is a figure; the per-weight counting elaborates the sketch)

name: Describe the online algorithm and stochastic (minibatch) gradient descent for an MLP, and compare them with the batch algorithm.
answer:
Online algorithm. It computes a sequence of weight vectors w(0), w(1), w(2), …; the weights in w(0) are randomly initialized to values close to 0; in step t + 1:
wji(t+1) = wji(t) + Δwji(t), where Δwji(t) = −ε(t) · ∂Ek/∂wji(w(t)),
with learning rate 0 < ε(t) ≤ 1. The update uses the error Ek of a single training example k instead of the whole E. There are other variants determined by the selection of the training examples used for the error computation.

SGD (stochastic gradient descent with minibatches).
• the weights in w(0) are randomly initialized to values close to 0;
• in step t + 1 (t = 0, 1, 2, …):
  – choose (randomly) a set of training examples T ⊆ {1, …, p} (a minibatch);
  – compute w(t+1) = w(t) + Δw(t), where Δw(t) = −ε(t) · Σk∈T ∇Ek(w(t));
• 0 < ε(t) ≤ 1 is the learning rate in step t + 1; ∇Ek(w(t)) is the gradient of the error of example k.
The random choice of the minibatch is typically implemented by randomly shuffling all data and then choosing minibatches sequentially.

Comparison. Batch gradient descent uses T = {1, …, p} (the exact gradient of E, but every step costs a pass over the whole training set); the online algorithm uses a single example per step; SGD with minibatches lies in between – each step is cheap and uses only an estimate of the gradient.
keyPoints: Online: Δw_ji^(t) = −ε(t) · ∂E_k/∂w_ji – one training example per step
SGD: random minibatch T ⊆ {1..p}
Implemented by shuffling the data and taking minibatches sequentially
Batch = all examples per step; minibatch gradient is only an estimate
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 96–97 (batch algorithm: slide 87)

name: Which output activation and error function are typically used for regression and for multi-class classification? Give the formulas.
answer:
Regression.
• Output activation: typically the identity, i.e. yi = σ(ξi) = ξi for i ∈ Y.
• Training dataset {(xk, dk) | k = 1, …, p} with xk ∈ ℝ|X| and desired outputs dk ∈ ℝ|Y|, dk = (dki)i∈Y.
• Error function: mean squared error (mse)
E(w) = (1/p) Σk=1..p Ek(w), where Ek(w) = ½ Σi∈Y (yi(w, xk) − dki)2.

Classification.
• Output activation: softmax
yi = σi(ξj1, …, ξjk) = eξi / Σj∈Y eξj, where Y = {j1, …, jk}.
Unlike ordinary activations, softmax depends on the potentials of all output neurons; the outputs are positive and sum to 1, so they can be read as a probability distribution over the classes.
• Training dataset {(xk, dk) | k = 1, …, p} with xk ∈ ℝ|X| and dk ∈ {0,1}|Y| (the desired class is marked by 1).
• Error function: (categorical) cross-entropy
E(w) = −(1/p) Σk=1..p Σi∈Y dki log(yi(w, xk)).
keyPoints: Regression: identity output activation
MSE: E = (1/p) Σ_k ½ Σ_{i∈Y} (y_i − d_ki)²
Classification: softmax y_i = e^{ξ_i} / Σ_{j∈Y} e^{ξ_j}
Desired outputs d_k ∈ {0,1}^|Y|
Categorical cross-entropy: E = −(1/p) Σ_k Σ_{i∈Y} d_ki log y_i
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 98–99 (the probability reading of softmax is a standard remark, not printed on the slide)

name: Practical (derivation): For softmax outputs with the cross-entropy error, rewrite E(w) in terms of the outputs y<sub>ℓ</sub> of the layer V just below the output layer, and then compute ∂E/∂y<sub>ℓ</sub> for ℓ ∈ V (the lecture leaves this last step as an exercise).
answer:
Rewriting E (slide). Assume V is the layer just below the output layer Y, so ξi = Σℓ∈V wiℓyℓ for i ∈ Y. Then
E(w) = −(1/p) Σk Σi∈Y dki log(yi(w, xk))
= −(1/p) Σk Σi∈Y dki log( eξi / Σj∈Y eξj )
= −(1/p) Σk Σi∈Y dki ( ξi − log Σj∈Y eξj )
= −(1/p) Σk Σi∈Y dki ( Σℓ∈V wiℓyℓ − log Σj∈Y eΣℓ∈V wjℓyℓ ).

Completing the exercise (the slide stops at "Now compute the derivatives"; the following is the standard computation). Consider one training example k and differentiate the bracket w.r.t. yℓ:
• ∂(Σℓ'∈V wiℓ'yℓ')/∂yℓ = wiℓ;
• ∂(log Σj∈Y eξj)/∂yℓ = Σj∈Y eξj wjℓ / Σj'∈Y eξj' = Σj∈Y yj wjℓ.
Hence
∂Ek/∂yℓ = −Σi∈Y dki ( wiℓ − Σj∈Y yjwjℓ ).
If the desired outputs are one-hot (Σi∈Y dki = 1), this simplifies to
∂Ek/∂yℓ = Σj∈Y (yj − dkj) · wjℓ,
Since yℓ takes a different value for every example, the per-example derivative ∂Ek/∂yℓ is the well-defined quantity; the factor 1/p of E only rescales each of these terms.

Interpretation: compared with the general backpropagation formula Σr∈j→ ∂Ek/∂yr · σ′r(ξr) · wrj, the product "derivative of the error × derivative of the output activation" collapses to the simple difference yj − dkj, i.e. ∂Ek/∂ξj = yj − dkj for output neurons. Softmax cannot be handled by the per-neuron formula directly because each yi depends on all output potentials – that is why E is differentiated as a whole.
keyPoints: log softmax = ξ_i − log Σ_j e^{ξ_j}
Substitute ξ_i = Σ_{ℓ∈V} w_iℓ y_ℓ
Derivative of the log-sum-exp term w.r.t. y_ℓ is Σ_j y_j w_jℓ
∂E_k/∂y_ℓ = −Σ_i d_ki (w_iℓ − Σ_j y_j w_jℓ)
One-hot targets: ∂E_k/∂y_ℓ = Σ_{j∈Y} (y_j − d_kj) w_jℓ
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slide 100 (rewriting of E is on the slide; the final derivative is the exercise it poses, worked out here)

name: Describe the output activation and error function used for binary classification, and explain – with the single-neuron computation from the lecture – why cross-entropy is preferable to the squared error with a logistic output.
answer:
Binary classification. Assume a single output neuron o, Y = {o}.
• Output activation: logistic sigmoid σo(ξo) = eξo/(eξo + 1) = 1/(1 + e−ξo).
• Training dataset T = {(x1, d1), …, (xp, dp)}, where xk = (xk0, xk1, …, xkn) ∈ ℝn+1, xk0 = 1, is the k-th input and dk ∈ {0, 1} is the desired output.
• Error function: (binary) cross-entropy
E(w) = −Σk=1..p [ dk log(yo(w, xk)) + (1 − dk) log(1 − yo(w, xk)) ].

Squared error vs. cross-entropy. Consider a single-neuron model y = σ(w·x) = 1/(1 + e−w·x) with one weight w ∈ ℝ (no bias) and a training set T = {(x, d)}, x ∈ ℝ, d ∈ {0, 1}. Recall σ′ = y(1 − y).

Squared error E(w) = ½(y − d)2:
∂E/∂w = (y − d) · y · (1 − y) · x.
• If d = 1 and y ≈ 0, then ∂E/∂w ≈ 0 (factor y ≈ 0).
• If d = 0 and y ≈ 1, then ∂E/∂w ≈ 0 (factor 1 − y ≈ 0).
The gradient of E is small even though the model is wrong – the saturated sigmoid kills the gradient and learning stalls.

Cross-entropy E(w) = −d·log(y) − (1 − d)·log(1 − y):
• for d = 1: ∂E/∂w = −(1/y) · y · (1 − y) · x = −(1 − y) · x, which is close to −x for y ≈ 0;
• for d = 0: ∂E/∂w = −(1/(1 − y)) · (−y) · (1 − y) · x = y · x, which is close to x for y ≈ 1.
The factor y(1 − y) from the sigmoid derivative cancels, so the gradient is large exactly when the model is confidently wrong and the error is corrected quickly.
keyPoints: Single output with logistic sigmoid, d_k ∈ {0,1}
Binary cross-entropy: E = −Σ_k [d_k log y_o + (1 − d_k) log(1 − y_o)]
Squared error: ∂E/∂w = (y − d) · y(1 − y) · x ≈ 0 when the output is saturated and wrong
Cross-entropy, d = 1: ∂E/∂w = −(1 − y)x; d = 0: ∂E/∂w = y·x
The sigmoid derivative cancels → large gradient when the model is wrong

name: Define a computational graph and its semantics (how it is evaluated). Show how a k-layer MLP is expressed as a computational graph.
answer:
Computational graph. Consider a directed acyclic graph (V, E). Individual nodes are denoted by indices n, m, etc. For a node n, denote by n← the set of all nodes m such that (m, n) ∈ E and by n→ the set of all nodes m such that (n, m) ∈ E.
• input nodes are nodes with n← = ∅;
• output nodes are nodes with n→ = ∅;
• hidden nodes are the remaining nodes.
Each node n has its output value yn (in general a vector). Each non-input node n is assigned a function fn such that
yn = fn(yn1, …, ynk), where n← = {n1, …, nk} (assuming a fixed ordering on n←).

Semantics.
Input: a collection of vectors vn, one for each input node n.
Computation:
• start with yn = vn for every input node n;
• while there are nodes that have not been evaluated: select a node n all of whose predecessors have been evaluated and compute yn = fn(yn1, …, ynk).
Output: the collection of values of all output nodes (a collection of vectors).
Because the graph is acyclic, such a node always exists until all nodes are evaluated.

k-layer MLP as a graph. Take the chain graph with V = {0, 1, …, k} and E = {(n − 1, n) | n = 1, …, k}. Each node n = 1, …, k is a whole layer and is assigned the function
yn = fn(yn−1) = σn(Wnyn−1),
where Wn is a weight matrix and σn is a vector of activation functions applied component-wise: for σn = (σn1, …, σnr) we have σn(x1, …, xr) = (σn1(x1), …, σnr(xr)). The input node 0 gets a vector as input and the output node k gives a vector as output.
keyPoints: Directed acyclic graph; n← predecessors, n→ successors
Input nodes: n← = ∅; output nodes: n→ = ∅; others hidden
Each non-input node has a function f^n: y^n = f^n(y^{n_1}, …, y^{n_k})
Evaluate any node whose predecessors are all evaluated, until done
MLP: chain 0 → 1 → … → k with y^n = σ^n(W^n y^{n−1})

name: How is differentiation defined between two connected nodes of a computational graph? Define the Jacobian matrix ∂y<sup>n</sup>/∂y<sup>m</sup> and compute it for the layers of the MLP graph.
answer:
We are interested in the rate of change of yn based on changes in ym, i.e. the derivative of yn w.r.t. ym.

Jacobian. Given two nodes n and m such that (m, n) ∈ E, with yn having I components and ym having J components, ∂yn/∂ym denotes the I × J Jacobian matrix obtained by differentiating each component of yn w.r.t. each component of ym:
             | dy^n_1/dy^m_1  dy^n_1/dy^m_2  ...  dy^n_1/dy^m_J |
dy^n/dy^m =  | dy^n_2/dy^m_1  dy^n_2/dy^m_2  ...  dy^n_2/dy^m_J |
             |      ...            ...       ...       ...      |
             | dy^n_I/dy^m_1  dy^n_I/dy^m_2  ...  dy^n_I/dy^m_J |
More concretely, the ij element is
∂yni/∂ymj = ∂(fn(yn1, …, ynk))i / ∂ymj,
meaning that the value yni of yn is differentiated w.r.t. ymj. Rows correspond to components of the output of node n, columns to components of the output of node m.

MLP example. In the k-layer MLP graph ({0, 1, …, k}, {(n − 1, n) | n = 1, …, k}) with yn = fn(yn−1) = σn(Wnyn−1), the Jacobian is
∂yn/∂yn−1 = σ̇n Wn,
where σ̇n is the diagonal matrix of derivatives of the components of σn: for σn = (σn1, …, σnr), σ̇n = diag(σ̇n1, …, σ̇nr), with the derivatives evaluated at the inner potentials Wnyn−1 of the layer.

Check with components: yni = σni(Σj Wnij yn−1j), so ∂yni/∂yn−1j = σ̇ni · Wnij, which is exactly the ij entry of σ̇nWn – the same quantity σ′r(ξr) · wrj that appears in the neuron-level backpropagation formula.
keyPoints: ∂y^n/∂y^m is the Jacobian: entry (i, j) = ∂y^n_i/∂y^m_j
Defined for nodes with (m, n) ∈ E; I × J matrix
MLP layer: ∂y^n/∂y^{n−1} = σ̇^n W^n
σ̇^n = diagonal matrix of activation derivatives
Entry (i, j) = σ̇^n_i · W^n_ij, matching σ′_r(ξ_r) · w_rj

name: Formulate backpropagation for general computational graphs, and apply it to the MLP graph extended by an error node to obtain the layer-wise backward recursion.
answer:
General backpropagation. Fix a node o. Our aim is to compute ∂yo/∂yn for all predecessors n of o in the computational graph.
• Base: ∂yo/∂yo = I, the identity matrix.
• Recursion: by the (appropriately general version of the) chain rule,
∂yo/∂yn = Σm∈n→ (∂yo/∂ym) · (∂ym/∂yn),
a sum over all successors m of n of products of Jacobian matrices.
• Now propagate the gradient from o to all its predecessors n: a node can be processed once ∂yo/∂ym is known for all its successors m, i.e. the nodes are processed in the reverse of the evaluation order. The local Jacobians ∂ym/∂yn are evaluated at the values computed in the forward evaluation of the graph.

MLP with an error node. Consider the MLP graph with one additional "error" node:
• V = {0, 1, …, k, o}, E = {(n − 1, n) | n = 1, …, k} ∪ {(k, o)};
• each node n = 1, …, k is assigned yn = fn(yn−1) = σn(Wnyn−1);
• fo is the error function (e.g. the squared error) applied to the network output yk.

Backprop:
• ∂yo/∂yk is the derivative of the error function (for the squared error the row vector with entries yj − dkj);
• for n ≤ k, every node n − 1 has the single successor n, so
∂yo/∂yn−1 = (∂yo/∂yn) · (∂yn/∂yn−1) = (∂yo/∂yn) · σ̇nWn.

Starting at the top and multiplying by σ̇nWn layer by layer gives the derivative of the error w.r.t. the outputs of every layer – the matrix form of the neuron-level rule ∂Ek/∂yj = Σr∈j→ ∂Ek/∂yr · σ′r(ξr) · wrj.
keyPoints: Fix node o; compute ∂y^o/∂y^n for all predecessors n
Base case: ∂y^o/∂y^o = I
Chain rule: ∂y^o/∂y^n = Σ_{m∈n→} (∂y^o/∂y^m)(∂y^m/∂y^n)
MLP graph plus error node o with edge (k, o); f^o = error function
∂y^o/∂y^{n−1} = (∂y^o/∂y^n) · σ̇^n W^n, starting from the derivative of the error
